title: How (O)possums Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore possums (opossums), focusing on the Virginia possum, the only marsupial native to the United States. They cover marsupial evolution and the fossil record (possums as ancestors of Australian marsupials), the naming confusion with Australian possums (Joseph Banks, 1770), the word's Algonquin origin, American range expansion, physical traits (naked tail and ears, size, teeth), a small brain relative to body size, intelligence tests, diet and value as a tick and pest eater, denning and tail-carrying behavior, short lifespan, reproduction with many tiny young that climb into the pouch, the forked penis and multiple vaginas, playing dead, bluffing and hissing, possums as pets, eating possum as Southern food and presidential anecdotes, and possum venom resistance with the LTNF protein that may help treat snake bite. The episode also includes a host story about a possum on a porch, a listener mail about Gordon Lightfoot and yum-yucking, and a sponsor-style break.

segments.title: Opening banter and Instagram request
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show title and an Instagram follower who repeatedly asked for a possum episode, which is the reason for this one.

segments.title: Marsupials and possum evolution
segments.summary: Hosts explain that possums are marsupials and that marsupials likely descended from North or South American possums, spreading to Australia via South America and Antarctica. They describe the Panamanian land bridge letting possums return to North America about a million years ago, and note that Australian possums are a different animal.

segments.title: Possum name and Joseph Banks confusion
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the word opossum, which comes from an Algonquin word meaning white beast or white dog, and explain that naturalist Joseph Banks, who went to Australia with James Cook in 1770, mislabeled the Australian bush tail possum as the same animal as the American possum.

segments.title: Range and spread across the United States
segments.summary: The Virginia possum originally lived in the southeast and spread through the nineteenth century as farms and cities grew, with some moved by people to places like Washington State. Its range now covers much of the eastern and southern US, parts of the Midwest, and extends into Ontario and Canada.

segments.title: Physical traits and cold tolerance
segments.summary: Possums have naked tails and ears that are prone to frostbite, so they use human structures such as wall voids for shelter in cold months. Virginia possums weigh about four to eleven pounds, measure two to three feet with tail, and are whitish gray.

segments.title: Anatomy and forked penis
segments.summary: The hosts discuss possum anatomy, including the forked penis, which relates to the female having two vaginas for mating and a third for giving birth. They joke about old colonial myths and look at a picture.

segments.title: Small brain and surprising intelligence
segments.summary: Possums have one of the smallest brain-to-body ratios among mammals, measured by how many dried beans fit in the skull. Despite this, they beat rats, rabbits, dogs and cats in food-location and maze tests, and remember foods that made them sick.

segments.title: Diet, cleanliness, rabies resistance and pest control
segments.summary: Possums eat nearly anything, including insects, worms, small mammals, carrion, fruit and garbage, and are often blamed unfairly for garbage can raids. They are clean, have low body temperatures that make rabies unlikely, and eat thousands of ticks in a season, along with slugs and mice.

segments.title: Dens, tails, lifespan and reproduction
segments.summary: Possums rehab abandoned dens and line them with leaves, carry materials with their prehensile tails, and can travel miles; they do not sleep hanging upside down. They live about two to three years, and females have many young, some of which are abandoned. Newborns are tiny, emerge deaf and blind, and climb into the pouch using smell and gravity.

segments.title: Playing possum, hissing and bluffing
segments.summary: Possums hiss and bluff when cornered and, as a last resort, involuntarily play dead, going limp, drooling and releasing foul fluid. Predators often lose interest. Possums have about fifty teeth.

segments.title: Host porch story
segments.summary: Chuck shares a personal story about a possum trapped under a porch railing when he was in high school, and another about his father carrying a possum out of a woodpile in Ohio.

segments.title: Possums as pets, food and presidents
segments.summary: Possums make poor pets and rescues sometimes end up as YouTube pets. Historically, Southern families ate possum, often fattening them on milk and cereal first, and presidents such as Jimmy Carter, Taft, Washington and Jefferson had connections to possums. The Teddy Bear and the Billy Possum toy are mentioned.

segments.title: Possum venom resistance and listener mail, sign-off
segments.summary: Possums resist snake venom through a protein called LTNF that may help treat snake bite. A listener mail about Gordon Lightfoot and yum-yucking is read, and the hosts sign off.
